name: Lena Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on the grid upgrade crew out of the Westfield depot. We're fitting the old overhead network with smart switches and sensors, so when a branch hits a line, the system can cut off just that bit and reroute power around it instead of a whole town going dark. A normal day is two or three installs: up the pole, mount the switch, wire it, then test it with the control room on the radio. I love that it's new, it feels like we're building something rather than just patching. What wears me out is when the control room software crashes and we're stuck at the top of a pole waiting for someone to reboot it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home? What's your life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rob is a freelance photographer, weddings and some company work, and our kids are Hannah, fifteen, and Leo, twelve. We've got a mortgage on an old house we're slowly doing up and about four months of savings, though Rob's income goes up and down a lot. His company work has already dried up a bit because businesses make their own pictures with AI now. I use AI every day, for planning installs, reading manuals, even arguing with it about the best way to route a cable. I'm not very political, I like ideas that work, whoever has them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame in some ways, because I find the tools useful. But I'd probably post something like, good, now we can get back to fixing things. I'd say the real work was always going to be on the poles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. The smart grid upgrades are happening anyway, because of all the solar and electric cars, so my work's steady. And maybe Rob's company clients come back, if the AI pictures turn out to be not quite good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my job and keep using AI for planning and manuals. Maybe push to get onto the control room training, because that's where the smart grid work is heading. Keep saving a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of disappointment, honestly. I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the control room training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every switch I install feeds data back to the control room, and they're short of people who know what the kit looks like up close. I'd like to be the person who understands both ends. And my knees won't climb poles forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Rob's clients might come back. Do you think they would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, maybe. The wedding work is fine, people still want a person there on the day. The company work, I'm less sure. Even in a hype-only world, some of that's gone for good.

S0.say: It's a shame in some ways because the tools are useful, but good, now we can get back to fixing things. The real work was always going to be on the poles.
S0.think: Her work is steady because smart grid upgrades are happening anyway for solar and electric cars. She hopes some of Rob's company clients come back if AI pictures fall short.
S0.do: Keeps working on smart switch installs and using AI for planning and manuals. Pushes to get onto control room training and keeps saving a bit each month.
S0.feel: Calm, with a little disappointment, because she likes new toys.
S0.quote: I'd like to be the person who understands both ends. And my knees won't climb poles forever.
S0.fieldNote: Lena already works at the leading edge of grid change and enjoys it. Her household has felt AI's bite through her partner's photography work. She's thinking ahead about her body and the next role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people can handle it if the training's there. I'd tell the crew to get ahead of it, not wait to be told. Online I'd probably share the things that worked for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be good for my job and bad for Rob's. I'm already on the crew installing the automated kit, so I'm in a good spot. But his photography work would shrink more, and his income's already patchy. That's the bit that'd bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every pilot, the inspection drones, the AI fault planner, whatever they're testing, and help roll them out to other crews. I'd apply for the control room training in the first six months. And I'd help Rob set up a better website and lean into weddings and events, where people still want a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, worrying for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'good for me, worrying for us'. How does that play out at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means more of the bills land on me. Right now Rob covers maybe a third. If that dropped to a fifth, we'd manage, but we'd stop the house work for a while. The kitchen would stay half done, which Hannah would never let me forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, my crew leader, who's brilliant on the pole but can't stand screens. He'd fight the new tools and the managers would see it. I'd try to make it easy for him, sit with him on the tablet and that.

S1.say: It's a big change, but people can handle it if training is there. She'd tell the crew to get ahead of it and share online what worked for her.
S1.think: It would be good for her job, since she's already installing the automated kit, but bad for Rob's patchy photography income. That household squeeze is what bothers her.
S1.do: Volunteers for every pilot, from inspection drones to the AI fault planner, and helps roll them out to other crews. Applies for control room training within six months and helps Rob shift toward weddings and events.
S1.feel: Uneasy: good for her, worrying for the household.
S1.quote: The kitchen would stay half done, which Hannah would never let me forget.
S1.fieldNote: Her unease comes from the household, not her own job. She actively brings new tools into her crew's work. She wants to help her less tech-minded crew leader rather than overtake him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast for anyone to handle well, so the priority is keeping people afloat while it settles. I'd say that calmly at work, because people would be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years means my head start doesn't matter much. If AI can run the control room and robots can mount the switches, then the jobs I was moving toward go too. And Rob's work would be mostly gone. We'd be living on four months of savings and whatever my job lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd stop the house project and cut spending to the basics. I'd look for the jobs that would last longest, maybe in the team that commissions and checks the robots, and I'd apply the minute I saw one. Rob and I would look at whether he could retrain fast, maybe as a teaching assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel like I could do something, but I'd be scared for the four of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest with her, she'd see through anything else. I'd say the world's changing faster than anyone expected, and we're going to be careful with money for a while. And I'd ask her what she wants to do, because her answer would matter more now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, what would you try to get in place before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Any certificate that gets me onto robot commissioning, as fast as I could. I'd pay for it if I had to. Even if it only buys a year or two, that's a year or two of income while Rob finds his feet.

S2.say: It's going too fast for anyone to handle well, so the priority is keeping people afloat while it settles. She'd say it calmly because others would be panicking.
S2.think: Two years erases her head start, because AI could run the control room and robots could mount switches. With Rob's work mostly gone, they'd be living on four months of savings.
S2.do: Stops the house project, cuts spending to basics and saves what she can. Applies at once for robot commissioning roles and pays for a certificate if needed, while Rob looks at fast retraining as a teaching assistant.
S2.feel: Anxious, still able to act but scared for the four of them.
S2.quote: Even if it only buys a year or two, that's a year or two of income while Rob finds his feet.
S2.fieldNote: Even as the most tech-ready person on her crew, the fast timeline pushes her into survival mode. She stays action-focused and avoids panic. Her daughter's views on the future matter to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but enough to move people sensibly, if companies start retraining now. I'd want the government to fund courses and to keep an eye on safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to get into the control room, then onto the robot side, and be one of the people checking their work. Hannah would be twenty, Leo seventeen. Rob would have time to change direction too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Control room training next year, then whatever robot commissioning course appears. Save an extra two hundred a month and pay down the mortgage a bit faster. Rob would retrain, maybe as a teaching assistant or in photo restoration for museums, something with people or old things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay down the mortgage rather than build savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really, but a smaller mortgage is less to worry about if we both lose work around 2031. Savings run out. A paid-off chunk of house doesn't. I've done the sums on a spreadsheet, and the AI helped me check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the five years change for Rob?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. In two years he's just out of work. In five he can try a couple of things and see what sticks. He's slower to change than me, so the time matters more for him than for me.

S3.say: Five years is tight but enough to move people sensibly if companies start retraining now. The government should fund courses and keep watch on safety.
S3.think: Five years is enough to move into the control room and then the robot side, checking their work. It also gives Rob time to change direction.
S3.do: Starts control room training next year and takes a robot commissioning course when one appears. Saves an extra two hundred a month and overpays the mortgage, while Rob retrains in something people-based.
S3.feel: Uneasy, in a way she can work with.
S3.quote: Savings run out. A paid-off chunk of house doesn't.
S3.fieldNote: Lena treats the five-year picture as a project for the whole household. She sees the extra time as mattering more for her partner than for herself. She used AI to check her own financial plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway, so let's be grown-ups about it: training money, honest timelines from companies, and help for people who can't move as fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be alright. I'd be 53, the kids grown. I'd have done the control room, then the robot side, maybe ending up teaching or inspecting. And we've already been through Rob's work drying up, so we know how to do this as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, slower: control room training in a year or two, then build from there. I'd put some savings into a pension top-up and maybe a small index fund. We'd help the kids pick studies that mix tech and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's a big change, but there's time to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'we know how to do this as a family'. What did you learn from Rob's work drying up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you have to talk about money out loud, at the kitchen table, every month. And that you should change direction before you're forced to. Rob waited too long with the company clients, and it cost us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys who won't move, like Pete. Ten years sounds like a lot, but if you spend eight of them hoping it won't happen, it's two years again. I'd keep nagging him.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent runway, so be grown-ups about it: training money, honest company timelines and help for people who can't move as fast.
S4.think: She thinks they'd be alright: at 53 with grown kids, she'd move through the control room and robot side to teaching or inspecting. The family already learned from Rob's work drying up.
S4.do: Follows the same plan more slowly, starting control room training in a year or two. Puts some savings into a pension top-up and a small index fund, and helps the kids choose studies that mix tech and people.
S4.feel: Calm, mostly, with time to steer.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like a lot, but if you spend eight of them hoping it won't happen, it's two years again.
S4.fieldNote: Her calm in the long picture comes partly from having already lived through her partner's work shrinking. She believes in changing direction early. Her remaining worry is for colleagues who will wait.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out my head start and Rob's work at the same time. What would help is fast, paid training for the jobs that last, robot commissioning and inspection, and some income support while people are in between. Short courses, not three-year degrees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partner. Everyone asks about my job, but in our house the AI change already happened to Rob first. I'd want people to know it doesn't always start with the person you'd expect.

headlineQuote: In our house the AI change already happened to Rob first.
portrait: Lena Baker is a 43-year-old lineworker on a grid upgrade crew, fitting smart switches and sensors, who uses AI every day and enjoys being where the new technology arrives. Her partner Rob is a freelance photographer whose company work has already shrunk because of AI, so their household has felt the change before her job has. Steady change looks good for her career but worrying for their income, and fast AGI wipes out her head start and pushes her into survival mode. With five or ten years she becomes calm and methodical, planning a move into the control room and robot commissioning and helping Rob change direction early.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would wipe out her head start and Rob's remaining work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, paid short courses for lasting roles like robot commissioning and inspection, plus income support while people are between jobs.
